documents.abstract: The accelerating digitisation of higher education has prompted urgent questions about which technology-mediated pedagogical interventions most effectively improve student learning outcomes in scientific disciplines. Drawing on a cross-institutional survey of 1500 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in STEM and scientific programmes across five institution types, this study investigates the individual and joint effects of three canonical digital transformation mechanisms: virtual simulation laboratories (VSL), artificial intelligence-assisted learning (AIAAL), and blended teaching models (BTM). Employing a mixed-methods empirical framework that combines structural equation modelling (SEM), multi-level fixed-effects regression, and bootstrap mediation analysis, we estimate standardised direct effects of 0.264, 0.218, and 0.192 for VSL, AIAAL, and BTM on academic achievement, respectively. Mediation analysis reveals that self-regulated learning (SRL), collaborative knowledge construction, and cognitive engagement jointly channel 55.5% of the VSL effect and 54.7% of the AIAAL effect through indirect pathways, underscoring the primacy of process-level learning mechanisms. Moderation analysis demonstrates that institutional readiness amplifies all three technology effects by 42-68%, while disciplinary context generates the sharpest differential: VSL effects in STEM disciplines are 110% larger than in non-STEM contexts, whereas AIAAL effects remain comparably robust across disciplines. Robustness tests using instrumental variables, propensity score matching, and difference-in-differences quasi-experimental designs confirm that results are not artefacts of selection bias or omitted variable contamination. Policy scenario projections to 2030 suggest that full digital integration could reduce inter-institutional achievement gaps by 74% relative to business-as-usual. The findings contribute a theoretically grounded and empirically validated framework for evidence-based digital transformation in scientific higher education.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping how political campaigns are produced and circulated. In Nigeria, parties, candidates, and supporters now rely heavily on digital tools to create adverts, images, and voice messages, yet little is known about how ordinary electorates in South-South Nigeria read such content. This exploratory study therefore examined how registered voters in South-South Nigeria distinguish AI-generated from human-created campaign messages, explain their trust or distrust in them, and describe their emotional responses and possible voting intentions ahead of the 2027 elections. A qualitative exploratory design was used. Nineteen registered voters aged 18–40 who actively use social media were purposively selected for maximum variation. Data were collected through online semi-structured interviews using six campaign messages, along with observation notes, and analysed with reflexive thematic analysis. Participants identified AI mainly through unnatural movement, implausible settings and contextual inconsistencies. Human-created messages were generally trusted more, although emotionally relevant AI content could also appear credible. Emotional reactions included humour, hope, confusion and worry, but these rarely translated directly into voting intention. Within this sample, recognition, trust and voting responses depended on realism, relevance, prior knowledge and candidate credibility. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger, representative studies.

documents.abstract: Single-Pilot Operations (SPO) in commercial aviation raise critical safety challenges in complex, time-pressured situations where human expertise is paramount. This study investigates how AI-based Human-Autonomy Teaming (HAT) can support pilot decision-making under high workload, compromised situational awareness, and time pressure. In a high-fidelity Airbus A320 simulator, 22 airline pilots performed a fuel- and time-constrained approach scenario designed to challenge HAT’s operational effectiveness under four conditions: no assistance, on-demand AI, proactive AI, and proactive explainable AI. Workload (NASA-TLX) remained high across conditions, yet decision-making differed markedly. Without assistance, only 20% chose the safest landing option; with on-demand AI, 40%; and with proactive AI (both versions), 100%. Explainable AI yielded the highest scenario comprehension (75%), matching two-crew baseline performance. Proactive systems increased decision and SA related interactions, fostering a collaborative dynamic akin to traditional crew resource management. Thus, the results demonstrate that, in the context of SPO, proactive and explainable AI was associated with crew-level decision performance within the experimental scenario without adding cognitive load. Beyond the aeronautical domain, our results are of interest for the design of cognitive support systems for high-risk domains where teams composed of humans and AI must adapt in real time.

Teachers' limited competence in utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based digital media has hindered the effective implementation of innovative teaching practices and environmental projects. This community service program aimed to enhance teachers' knowledge and skills in developing AI-based instructional media. The program was conducted at State Senior High School 1 Koto Kampar Hulu and involved 29 teachers through educational seminars, workshops, hands-on practice, and mentoring using Canva AI, Gemini AI, and NotebookLM. Program effectiveness was evaluated using pretest-posttest assessments, N-Gain analysis, instructional media product evaluation, and participant satisfaction questionnaires. The results showed that the participants' mean score increased from 47.0 to 78.9, with an N-Gain score of 0.6, indicating a moderate level of improvement. All participants (100%) demonstrated increased knowledge following the training. Furthermore, every participant successfully developed at least one AI-based instructional medium, such as a poster or infographic, that was ready for implementation in classroom instruction and environmental projects. These findings indicate that the training effectively enhanced teachers' digital competencies and their ability to integrate AI technologies into teaching and learning practices

documents.abstract: Technical, social, avant-garde, global, and cognitive pressures are driving the adoption of new technologies characterized by constant updates and automation most notably generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents. While the stated intention is to augment and enhance human capabilities regarding complex challenges, skills, and critical thinking rather than replacing them recent empirical evidence suggests the actual trend is moving in the opposite direction, to the detriment of consumers. This study analyzes the flaws and risks stemming from the use and misuse of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose intervention frameworks before they become irreversibly entrenched in a fragile structure within the technology adoption cycle. It explores phenomena such as the atrophy of technical skills, the productivity paradox, cognitive offloading, over-reliance on automated systems, and the irony of automation, drawing on evidence from randomized controlled trials and large-scale surveys conducted between 2025 and 2026. This analysis examines the critical failures and systemic risks of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose regulatory and operational intervention frameworks before their negative effects become irreversibly embedded in the labor market and social fabric. Identifying these risk vectors early allows for the design of guidelines that restore human control, ensuring technology acts as a genuine complement rather than an agent of cognitive and professional erosion. Furthermore, there is high demand for courses, diploma programs, and workshops focused on critical thinking, reflecting a growing awareness of the need to pursue them.

The article examines the evolution of UX/UI design tools in the context of the rapid development of the contemporary digital environment. The principal stages in the transformation of digital interface design tools are considered, from traditional graphic editors and static layouts to specialised UX/UI platforms, interactive prototyping, cloud-based environments, component-based design, and design systems. The impact of digital technologies on the organisation of UX/UI design processes is analysed, including the spread of collaborative tools, the integration of design into software development workflows, and the automation of individual design stages. Particular attention is paid to the current phase of UX/UI tool development associated with artificial intelligence, generative design, and AI-assisted workflows. The main trends in the further development of UX/UI design tools and the transformation of the designer’s professional role are identified. It is argued that digital design tools are evolving towards the integration of design, prototyping, user research, software development, and artificial intelligence within a unified environment aimed at creating effective, accessible, and personalised user experiences.

Abstract Integrating self-determination theory and regulatory focus theory, the study investigated how intrinsic and extrinsic motivation differentially influence teacher burnout through two types of job crafting behaviors. Survey data were collected from 480 primary and junior school teachers in China. Hierarchical regression analyses and PROCESS macro analyses were used to test the hypothesized model. Results indicated that intrinsic motivation diminished job burnout through promotion-focused job crafting (β = −0.13, p < 0.01), whereas extrinsic motivation intensified job burnout through prevention-focused job crafting (β = 0.31, p < 0.001). Furthermore, teaching experience negatively moderated these mediated pathways, with stronger indirect effects for novice teachers that attenuated as experience increased. These findings provide empirical support for career-stage-specific burnout interventions, suggesting that support strategies should be tailored to teachers' motivational profiles and professional development stages.

Machine learning models are now widely used to forecast stock price movements and to measure financial risk, yet most cannot explain their own outputs. In finance that is a serious weakness, because forecasts influence real investment decisions and regulators expect firms to justify the models they use. This review asks how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been applied to stock trend prediction and risk as-sessment, and how far the resulting explanations can be trusted. We first outline the economic theory of predictability and the standard risk measures, then set out the mathematics of the main explanation methods: Shapley-value attribution, LIME, gradient-based attribution, attention, and counterfactuals. We then compare representative studies, summarise regulatory expectations, and propose a five-layer framework for explainable forecasting. Across the literature we find that explanations are most useful as a validation tool, and that they become un-reliable when features are correlated, when markets change regime, or when a model is overfitted. Evidence that expla-nations improve decisions remains thin. We close with open problems, including causal explanation, shared benchmarks, and monitoring of explanations in production.

documents.abstract: Instructional activities that satisfy basic psychological needs can promote enjoyment and intrinsic motivation in learning. This instrumental study assessed the psychometric properties of the Spanish-adapted Sport Satisfaction Instrument (SSI-PE) within the context of physical education and examined its measurement invariance across sex among Mexican students. Participants included a total of 515 secondary school students from the cities of Chihuahua, Aldama, and Cuauhtémoc in the State of Chihuahua, Mexico; of these, 259 (50.3%) were males and 256 (49.7%) were females, and their ages ranged between 12 and 15 years (M = 13.15, SD = 0.86). Confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance by sex, and calculation of Pearson’s correlation coefficients were conducted to assess convergent validity. The seven-item model, the SSI-PE7, demonstrated more robust fit indices (GFI = 0.985, RMSEA = 0.047, and CFI = 0.990) and acceptable reliability (α = 0.84 for the satisfaction/fun factor and α = 0.74 for boredom). Measurement invariance analysis evidenced its applicability regardless of sex. Convergent validity showed that satisfaction/fun had a positive correlation with task orientation and ego, while the boredom factor had a negative correlation with the other scales. The findings suggest that the SSI-PE7 is a promising and reliable provisional instrument to assess students’ level of satisfaction with physical education classes.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges the university model centered on content transmission and subsequent testing. Large language models can retrieve, synthesize, and recombine information within seconds, but rapid access to information does not constitute reliable knowledge. This conceptual article argues that higher education should shift toward epistemic construction: the process of framing problems, integrating information, verifying sources, exposing assumptions, confronting counterarguments, revising provisional judgments, and defending conclusions. Drawing on Socratic inquiry, medieval disputatio, Popperian falsification, reflective learning, critical-thinking research, and scholarship on artificial intelligence in education, the study proposes the AI-Assisted Epistemic Construction Cycle. The framework positions generative AI not primarily as an answer-producing device, but as a scalable digital devil’s advocate that supports structured intellectual dissent. Implications are developed for faculty roles, student agency, assessment, institutional governance, academic integrity, and future research.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is changing university students' learning experiences, but how cognitive dispositions translate into sustained engagement in AI‐supported learning remains insufficiently understood. Guided by the Study Demands–Resources Model, this study examines the association between critical thinking disposition and learning engagement, with learning motivation, academic buoyancy, and grit as parallel indirect pathways. Using cross‐sectional data from 729 university students with experience using AI for learning, structural equation modelling tested the direct and indirect relationships among the variables, after which psychological network analysis identified central and bridge nodes within the learning psychological system. Critical thinking disposition was conceptualised as a cognitive personal resource, and learning motivation as a motivational resource. Academic buoyancy captured students' capacity to manage everyday academic setbacks, whereas grit represented perseverance in pursuing long‐term learning goals. The combination of variable‐centred and network‐based analyses provided complementary views of how these resources relate to university students' engagement in AI‐supported learning.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how travelers search for information and plan trips, yet much of the existing research still focuses on technology adoption, trust, or continuance intentions rather than on the process through which an AI recommendation is checked and translated into an actual decision. This study explores how Vietnamese independent travelers use GenAI in trip planning, how they evaluate and verify AI outputs, and how they decide whether to accept, modify, or reject those recommendations. An exploratory qualitative design was employed, involving 28 participants who had used GenAI to plan a specific independent trip. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews and analyzed using the Gioia methodology. The findings suggest that GenAI is shifting from a search tool toward a co-planning partner; however, its outputs are rarely received entirely passively. Travelers engage in selective verification depending on perceived risk, information volatility, and decision reversibility, while calibrating their trust according to the task and prior experience. Four ways of integrating AI recommendations into travel decisions were identified: direct acceptance, acceptance after verification, modified acceptance, and rejection. The study therefore proposes the concept of “verified co-planning” and develops a process model in which verification and trust calibration connect AI recommendations with action. These findings extend process-based understanding of GenAI in tourism and clarify how travelers preserve agency as AI becomes more deeply embedded in travel planning.

Research on human thinking explains how thoughts arise and how decisions are made, but rarely asks how a thought becomes an action, how the way thinking begins can be trained, and what a thought is worth. This conceptual paper answers these questions from Kirdomicism, an action-centric philosophy. It introduces the thwaction, a thorough thought carried by will into effective action, with accountability for its result, summarised in the conceptual equation Thinking × Action = Avalrem, where Avalrem is the unit of action value. The paper argues that a decision is not the end of thinking but the middle of an action; that self-force, willpower developed into habit, carries thought into action; that thoughts arise from a life setting described by the Buddhist Five Aggregates, with each first thought unpredictable but the mind’s tendencies trainable through a tool-free daily thwaction cycle; and that a thought has no value until it becomes action. The paper engages research on the intention–behaviour gap, implementation intentions, habit, spontaneous thought, prospection, cognitive offloading to artificial intelligence and the economics of ideas, including proposals to pay people for their data. It offers 23 propositions classified as definitional, explanatory or normative, two new measures (the thwaction count and the thwaction rate), and a research agenda of five studies.

Sustainability is increasingly recognized as a critical component for ensuring a resilient and prosperous future. Its significance spans environmental preservation, economic stability, social equity, and business innovation. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into sustainability education and research is reshaping the landscape of how environmental, social, and economic challenges are understood and addressed. As global sustainability goals become increasingly important and urgent, AI offers the transformative potential to enhance educational practices and research. Several emerging trends are poised to shape the future of AI in sustainability education and research. Firstly, Future trends indicate a shift toward AI-powered personalised learning experiences, where adaptive platforms can tailor content to individual learners’ needs, thereby improving engagement and comprehension. Secondly, the fusion of AI with augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies promises to create immersive learning experiences. These tools can simulate complex environmental scenarios, providing students with interactive platforms to explore sustainability challenges firsthand. Thirdly, AI is increasingly being leveraged to tackle humanitarian and environmental challenges such as the use of Google’s Flood Hub, which forecasts floods in 80 countries, exemplify AI’s potential in enhancing disaster preparedness and response. Fourthly, the interaction of blockchain in AI can enhance data security and transparency in research. This integration ensures the integrity of academic records and facilitates trustworthy collaborations across institutions. Fifthly, AI-driven predictive models can anticipate environmental trends and inform proactive strategies. In education, such analytics can identify at-risk students and tailor interventions to improve retention and success rates. Despite the many potential trends in AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research , it is important to address ethical concerns such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the potential misuse of technology. Developing responsible future Trends In AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research requires that technological advancements benefit all stakeholders without causing harm. Institutions must implement frameworks that promote transparency, accountability, and fairness in AI applications, fostering trust and social acceptance. Therefore, incorporating sustainability into AI-driven education equips students with the knowledge and skills necessary to address future environmental challenges.

This paper examines who might legitimately bring political considerations into technology development, particularly in contexts where traditional government political actors are absent. Drawing on two generative AI academic-practitioner collaborations in South Africa (a civic participation tool review and a chatbot construction for research content), I draw attention to how digital inequality, funding dynamics, and interpersonal tensions shape knowledge production and decision-making in technology partnerships. The cases demonstrate examples of how technologist knowledge can be undervalued, particularly when it comes to considering the political dimensions of technology deployment. I also consider how poor interpersonal dynamics, which stem from technophobia and discomfort with technical expertise, may have a detrimental impact. These organisational-level challenges have significant implications for emerging AI governance frameworks that rely on collaborative risk assessments and impact evaluations. The paper proposes empathetic collaboration strategies between partners in a technology development process, and strategies that include explicit acknowledgment of inequality in African technology environments, clear communications, skills transfer, and shared normative visions focused on human wellbeing - rather than mere efficiency gains. Such approaches can constitute a resistance to technocapitalist obfuscation and enable more equitable co-creation of responsible AI systems amongst different actors.

documents.abstract: The rapid spread of AI chatbots has begun to reshape how university students plan, draft, revise, and evaluate academic writing. Although recent studies have examined students’ perceptions of generative AI in higher education, less is known about how students in regional Indonesian universities understand and use these tools, particularly when viewed across gender, age, and academic level. This study investigated the perceptions and reported use of AI chatbots among 267 students from four universities in East Kalimantan. A mixed-method survey design was used. Quantitative responses were analyzed through descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rho correlation, while open-ended responses were coded to identify the AI tools students reported using for academic writing. The results show that AI use was widespread, with 94.76% of respondents indicating that they had used AI in academic writing. Students generally held positive views of AI chatbots, especially for improving writing effectiveness, language quality, and the revision process. At the same time, their responses revealed continuing ethical and pedagogical uncertainty, particularly around learning, authorship, and the boundary between assistance and cheating. Correlation analysis showed weak relationships between students’ perceptions and gender, age, or semester, suggesting that AI chatbot use was broadly shared across demographic groups. The study offers regional evidence from Indonesian higher education and underscores the need for clearer AI literacy instruction, responsible-use guidelines, and process-based academic writing pedagogy.

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, raising questions about how cognitively substantive activity is distributed between learners and AI systems. Yet research on these cognitive implications remains fragmented across constructs and disciplinary conversations. This study maps the cognitive landscape of GenAI research in higher education through a computational literature review of 1,435 Scopus-indexed publications from 2023 to 2026. The analysis combined bibliometric mapping, theory-informed dictionary-based detection of ten cognitive constructs, temporal prevalence analysis, document-level co-occurrence and phi association analysis, and Structural Topic Modelling (STM). Critical thinking was the most prominently represented construct, followed by metacognition, while automation bias, cognitive load, memory and attention, cognitive dependency, and cognitive offloading formed less prominent but differentiated concerns. Although critical thinking and metacognition showed the highest raw co-occurrence, automation bias and cognitive dependency exhibited the strongest positive prevalence-adjusted association, demonstrating that construct prominence and relational specificity represent different properties of the literature. STM identified eight thematic structures and indicated increasing relative prominence of cognitive and theoretical modelling over the study period. Integrating these patterns, the study proposes cognitive mediation as an interpretive framework encompassing cognitive engagement, regulation, redistribution, and vulnerability. The findings suggest that a central challenge for higher education is not simply whether GenAI supports or undermines learning, but how cognitive responsibility is distributed and regulated in learner–AI interaction. The study provides a basis for research and pedagogical design concerned with preserving meaningful learner agency while integrating GenAI into higher-education learning and assessment.

documents.abstract: The U.S. Copyright Office has released its report Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability. This paper explores the copyrightability of AI-generated and AI-assisted works in the United States, focusing on that report and on the jurisprudence of human authorship. It examines the constitutional and statutory bases of human authorship, the importance of Burrow-Giles, Feist, Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid and Thaler v. Perlmutter, and how the Copyright Office has dealt with prompting, human-authored inputs, selection, arrangement, modification and the assistive use of AI. The paper shows that the United States has adopted a case-by-case approach: the use of AI as a tool does not defeat protection, but copyright extends only to expression created by a human author and not to material generated by AI itself. Under current technology, prompts alone do not generally provide sufficient control, but human expression that is perceptible in the output, creative selection and arrangement, and meaningful modification can be protected. The paper sets out the strengths and weaknesses of this approach and suggests more explicit registration, evidentiary and guidance practices, while maintaining the human-authorship requirement.

1. Introduction Generative AI (GenAI) such as ChatGPT is now part of students’ academic life, raising concerns about dependency. Goh et al. (2025) define GenAI dependency as a pattern of cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, and withdrawal, not merely excessive use. A key concern is critical thinking, the logical, rational, and reflective evaluation of information, which may weaken when weighing and concluding are handed over to machines (Gerlich, 2025; Zhai et al., 2024). Findings in Indonesia are inconsistent: one study reports a negative effect (Nurcahyani & Noviani, 2026), another a strong positive relationship (Putra & Astuti, 2025). The independent variable is GenAI dependency; the dependent variable is critical thinking ability. 2. Objectives and Hypotheses Objectives: (1) describe levels of GenAI dependency and critical thinking; (2) test their relationship; (3) test whether it holds after controlling for semester and GenAI use intensity. H₁: GenAI dependency is negatively related to critical thinking ability. H₂: This negative relationship remains after controlling for semester and the frequency and duration of GenAI use. H₀: There is no significant relationship. Tests are two-tailed because some earlier findings are positive. A significant positive relationship will be reported as contradicting the hypothesis. 3. Design Quantitative, correlational, cross-sectional online survey. It tests relationships, not causation. Semester, weekly frequency, and daily duration of GenAI use are control variables. 4. Sample Population and technique: Active undergraduate students from various faculties and study programs at Universitas Negeri Surabaya; purposive sampling through [recruitment channel]. Sample size: G*Power (two-tailed correlation, α = 0.05, power = 0.80, r = 0.25) gives a minimum N of 123. Target: about 135 to allow for exclusions. Stopping rule: Collection stops at 135 valid responses or on [deadline date], whichever comes first. If N < 123, results are reported with a note on limited power. Inclusion: (a) active undergraduate; (b) used GenAI for academic purposes in the past three months; (c) informed consent. Exclusion: (1) duplicate responses (first kept); (2) incomplete main scales; (3) uniform responding (SD = 0 across GAIDS items); (4) not meeting inclusion (b). Exclusions are made before hypothesis testing and reported by reason. 5. Instruments GenAI dependency: Generative AI Dependency Scale (GAIDS; Goh et al., 2025), 11 items, 1–5 scale, three dimensions (cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, withdrawal); α = 0.92–0.93 in the original study. Score is the item mean; higher means greater dependency. Adapted to Indonesian by forward-backward translation and expert validation. Critical thinking: An Indonesian-language instrument of about 25 items measuring general critical thinking based on Bloom’s taxonomy; higher total score means better critical thinking. Selection criteria: general (not field-specific), α ≥ 0.70 among university students, clear score direction, and confirmed permission or license. The instrument’s name, scoring, and permission status will be added by amendment before data collection, and no data will be collected before permission is confirmed. Analyses use the total score, so they do not depend on the chosen instrument. Control variables: semester, weekly frequency, and daily duration of GenAI use. Age, gender, faculty/study program, and type of GenAI are collected for exploratory analysis. Psychometrics in this sample: three-factor CFA for GAIDS (good fit if CFI/TLI ≥ 0.90 and RMSEA/SRMR ≤ 0.08); corrected item-total correlations for critical thinking (r < 0.30 flagged, not removed); Cronbach’s α and McDonald’s ω ≥ 0.70 for both. If CFA fit is poor, the GAIDS total score is still used and this is reported as a limitation. 6. Analysis Plan Software: [SPSS/JASP]; α = 0.05, two-tailed. Descriptives (objective 1): mean, SD, range, and low/moderate/high categories (mean ± 1 SD). Assumptions: normality (Shapiro-Wilk), linearity, homoscedasticity. H₁ (objective 2): Pearson correlation (Spearman if assumptions fail) with 95% CI. Supported if the coefficient is negative and p < 0.05. H₂ (objective 3): partial correlation and hierarchical regression (Model 1: controls; Model 2: + GAIDS) with ΔR² and β. Supported if the GAIDS β remains negative and significant. If assumptions fail, robust standard errors or bootstrapping are used. Missing data and outliers: incomplete cases are excluded per the criteria; outliers are kept, with a sensitivity analysis without them. Exploratory: score differences by gender, semester, program cluster, and GenAI type. Deviations: Any deviation from the plan will be reported with reasons in the final manuscript.

The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created new opportunities to enhance active learning; however, empirical evidence regarding its integration with Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in Engineering Chemistry remains limited, particularly for simultaneously fostering Computational Thinking (CT) and chemistry achievement. This study investigates the effectiveness of integrating GenAI with PBL in an undergraduate Engineering Chemistry course within a Mechanical Engineering Education program. In the intervention, GPT-4 was embedded as an AI learning scaffold that guided students through Socratic questioning, provided formative feedback, and supported problem decomposition and analysis during collaborative PBL activities rather than supplying direct answers. Employing a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design, the study involved 68 undergraduate students (n = 34 experimental; n = 34 control) selected through cluster random sampling. Data were collected using three validated instruments: a Computational Thinking Test (CTT, 30 items, ? = .87), a Chemistry Achievement Test (CAT, 35 items, ? = .84), and a Learning Observation Sheet (LOS, 20 items, ICC = .91). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Levene's homogeneity tests, independent-samples t-tests, ANCOVA, and Cohen's d effect size analysis. The results revealed significant improvements in both CT skills (t(66) = 8.47, p .001) and chemistry achievement (t(66) = 9.12, p .001) in the experimental group compared with the control group. ANCOVA controlling for pretest scores confirmed significant treatment effects for CT (F(1,65) = 127.84, p .001) and chemistry achievement (F(1,65) = 109.07, p .001), with large practical effects (Cohen's d = 2.14 and 2.06, respectively). These findings provide empirical support for integrating AI-supported scaffolding within structured PBL environments to strengthen computational thinking and conceptual understanding in Engineering Chemistry, while extending the pedagogical application of AI-enhanced constructivist learning in engineering education.

documents.abstract: Introduction As AI evolves into agent-based forms, AI threat perception has become a defining workplace concern. Informed by Cognitive Appraisal Theory and Protection Motivation Theory, this cross-sectional study investigates how AI threat perception relates to post-adoptive AI agent engagement via dual paths of AI self-efficacy and defensive motivation. Methods Semi-structured interviews ( N = 13) first grounded scale adaptation. Structural equation modeling was then conducted on data collected from 387 knowledge workers, followed by multi-group analysis. Results The structural model demonstrates that AI threat perception is indirectly associated with post-adoptive engagement through both mediators, exhibiting an indirect-only pattern. Multi-group analysis further reveals demographic and contextual boundary conditions, showing that higher education significantly amplifies defensive motivation (the link is stronger among postgraduates), while exploratory career-stage and regional comparisons indicate that the self-efficacy pathway is stronger among early-to-mid career professionals and workers in eastern regions. Discussion The study highlights the concurrent coexistence of capability beliefs and defensive intentions in post-adoptive use, while pointing to the need for longitudinal research to trace their temporal dynamics. These findings refine our understanding of technology threat perception and inform human-agent collaboration.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) in marketing has prompted higher education institutions to invest substantially. However, a critical pedagogical question remains: whether and how these institutional investments translate into students’ psychological readiness to deploy AI tools effectively. Students’ AI self-efficacy constitutes a foundational prerequisite for technology adoption and career adaptability. A lack of such confidence can precipitate technology avoidance behaviors and diminish learning engagement. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a cognitive-mediation framework, this study investigates how perceived university support (PUS) shapes marketing students'’ AI self-efficacy (AISE) through the dual mediating beliefs of perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU),and whether this mechanism holds across institutionally heterogeneous settings. Using structural equation modeling with a sample of 538 marketing students from three Chinese universities, we find that PUS significantly enhanced both PU and PEOU in all samples,and that both beliefs carried the effect of support to self-efficacy.PU and PEOU mediated the PUS–AISE relationship: the indirect effect via PEOU was consistently stronger than that via PU,and the direct PUS–AISE path remained significant in two of the three institutions.This study bridges the gap between resource allocation and student psychological outcomes. The robust dual-mediation pathway offers actionable insights for universities: to build student confidence in AI, investments must be channeled not merely into infrastructure but also into pedagogical strategies that demonstrably reduce the perceived complexity of AI tools and illustrate the professional relevance of these tools.Limitations concerning the cross-sectional self-report design and the single-country sample are discussed.

Contemporary debates on artificial intelligence increasingly raise questions not only about machine agency but also about the nature of human creativity and freedom. While much of the current discussion evaluates AI by comparing its observable behaviour with that of human beings, this article argues that the decisive question is metaphysical rather than functional. Drawing on insights into the nature of freedom from Augustine, Aquinas, and other medieval theologians, I argue that human freedom arises from the rational creature’s participation in an immaterial mode of being that grounds the free agentic self-movement. This participatory account of freedom provides a theological anthropology capable of distinguishing human creativity from increasingly sophisticated artificial systems without appealing merely to current technological limitations. After examining two recent attempts to attribute free agency to AI systems, including theories rooted in intentionality and computational sourcehood, I argue that these accounts fail to identify the metaphysical conditions required for genuinely free and creative agency. Human freedom is shown to be inseparable from the unity of the spiritual soul, whose intellect and will participate in divine wisdom and providence with a specific kind of secondary causality. Thus, I identify the distinctive feature of human agentic intelligence in its intrinsic transcendent teleology, a mark of participation in the divine. AI systems, even their most autonomous future versions, seem limited by an intrinsic immanent teleology to their algorithmic boundaries. Thus, if my distinction holds, I determine that AI systems may increasingly reproduce the external operations associated with human intelligence and free agency, but they cannot participate in the kind of creative self-movement that belongs to rational creatures created in the image of God. The article concludes that the chief challenge posed by AI is therefore not whether machines will become human, but whether technological culture will encourage humanity to reinterpret itself according to computational categories rather than its vocation to participate in divine creativity.

Abstract Human-AI collaboration in emergency management represents a critical socio-technical challenge that requires understanding both technological capabilities and human factors. This study examines the barriers and enablers influencing emergency decision-makers’ adoption of generative artificial intelligence, focusing on the complex interplay between individual, organizational, and technological factors in high-stakes crisis environments. Through expert interviews and intuitionistic fuzzy DEMATEL analysis involving Chinese emergency management practitioners, we identify five key dimensions affecting AI adoption: technology acceptance, decision-making processes, contextual factors, risk and trust, and individual factors. Our analysis within the Chinese emergency management context suggests that contextual factors and decision-making processes are perceived as primary drivers, while technology acceptance and individual factors serve as critical enablers shaped by organizational environments. The findings demonstrate that successful human-AI collaboration requires addressing social and technical dimensions simultaneously, with organizational support, trust-building, and individual self-efficacy emerging as fundamental requirements. These insights inform strategies for emergency management organizations to enhance human-AI integration through governance frameworks, transparency mechanisms, and targeted training programs, contributing empirical evidence to the growing literature on socio-technical aspects of AI adoption in critical decision-making contexts.

Traditional enterprise automation systems often lack the contextual intelligence and flexibility required in logistics-intensive environments, particularly for small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SME). This paper proposes a fivephase implementation framework for Cognitive En- terprise Hubs (CEH), emphasizing role-sensitive deployment and continuous alignment between human and Artificial Intelligence (AI). The model combines architectural planning, AI integration and cultural adaptation to support scalable and adaptive collaboration across federated ecosystems. Empirical validation is provided through two crosssector case studies and a multi-role survey with 18 participants from IT, cybersecurity and telecommunications sectors. Findings reveal notable perceptual differences across organizational roles, especially between IT leaders, transformation strategists and frontline employees, regarding CEH impact on productivity, support and future opportunities. The study underscores that CEH success depends not only on technical orchestration but also on socio-cultural alignment. To address this, we offer practical deployment guidelines tailored for SME and logistics-driven operations. By integrating technical and organizational perspectives, this work advances the practical deployment of intelligent enterprise systems, positioning CEH as enablers of inclusive, cognitively enhanced coordination frameworks.

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Access to radiology and nuclear medicine remains profoundly unequal across global health systems. Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) face persistent shortages in imaging equipment, specialist workforce, digital infrastructure, maintenance, regulation and sustainable financing. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a mechanism to improve imaging access, but it may also reinforce existing inequities. This narrative review examines the potential for discriminative, generative and agentic AI to reduce or widen inequities in LMIC medical imaging and proposes a sociotechnical governance framework based on the concept of Humanity-in-the-Loop. KEY FINDINGS: Discriminative AI may improve image interpretation, triage, segmentation, quantification and image-quality assessment; generative AI may enhance reporting, education, translation, communication, synthetic data generation and research workflows; and agentic AI may coordinate referrals, scheduling, follow-up, supply logistics and imaging pathways. They may also exacerbate inequity through data colonialism, algorithmic under-performance, dataset shift, infrastructure dependence, commercial lock-in, second-tier automation, liability transfer and unequal participation in AI research and development. CONCLUSION: Human-in-the-loop governance is insufficient for equitable AI implementation in LMIC medical imaging because the assumptions underpinning effective human oversight are often absent in resource-constrained settings. The proposed Humanity-in-the-Loop sociotechnical framework embeds equity, local agency, contextual validity and public benefit throughout the AI lifecycle. The framework comprises six interconnected domains: patient humanity, workforce humanity, community humanity, data humanity, system humanity and global humanity. IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE: Responsible implementation of AI in medical imaging requires governance frameworks that extend beyond algorithm performance to include workforce development, data sovereignty, infrastructure, community priorities, equitable partnerships and sustainable capacity building. Adoption of a Humanity-in-the-Loop approach may help ensure that AI narrows rather than widens the medical imaging divide between high-income countries and LMICs.

documents.abstract: Hybrid Intelligence for Industrial Process Optimization: Establishing the Need Presentation delivered at the 23rd International Conference on Informatics in Control, Automation and Robotics (ICINCO 2026) within the Special Session on Hybrid Artificial Intelligence (HybAI 2026) held in Angers, France, October 26–28, 2026. Summary:Over 80% of industrial artificial intelligence proofs-of-concept (PoCs) stall or fail to reach production due to a fundamental structural mismatch: physical plants operate under rigorous thermodynamic and hydraulic conservation laws with zero fault tolerance, whereas pure data-driven machine learning models act as unconstrained black boxes omitting causal mechanisms. This presentation opens the HybAI 2026 Special Session by surveying the theoretical and practical imperatives for Hybrid Intelligence: Limits of Pure Data-Driven AI: Why the No Free Lunch theorem and severe physical exploration budgets make learning physics ab initio sample-inefficient and hazardous in production. Critique of Sutton's "Bitter Lesson": In digital games, simulation and trial-and-error exploration are computationally free; in municipal water systems and heavy industry, unconstrained exploration destroys hardware (pipe bursts, pump cavitation). Physical invariants are indispensable inductive scaffolds, not bottlenecks. Lessons from Neurorobotics: How biological motor control decomposes known morphological kinematics from state-dependent disturbance estimation, providing a direct design template for industrial gray-box digital twins. Acausal Physics & Differentiable SciML: Unifying Differential-Algebraic Equations (DAEs) with adjoint sensitivity analysis to guarantee safety and sample efficiency by design. documents.abstract: Understanding how university students perceive the development of their generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) skills over time can clarify how GenAI use relates to learning and academic outcomes. This study examined perceived skill-development trajectories, changes in learning practices, and associated academic gains using a retrospective questionnaire with 313 analyzed responses and interviews with 18 students across subject areas. Descriptive and comparative analyses and exploratory structural equation modeling (SEM) were integrated with thematic analysis. Perceived developmental trajectories were heterogeneous: 34.2% of students reported rapid early improvement followed by a plateau, 28.4% steady improvement, and 21.1% delayed acceleration. Development was also uneven across skills, with improvement in evaluating GenAI outputs perceived as more challenging; assignments were the most frequently selected driver of skill growth. Interviews further indicated increasingly specific prompting, tailored verification, and selective delegation, although some students reported stable routines, dependence, skipped reasoning, or improvements attributable partly to better GenAI tools. Academic gains were reported more often for assignments than for examinations. The SEM indicated a positive indirect association between perceived skill growth and academic gains through adaptation of assignment processes, whereas academic gains did not clearly differ across developmental trajectory groups after multiplicity correction. The findings suggest that perceived GenAI skill development varies in both trajectory and skill domain and is associated with changes in learning practices and differentiated academic benefits.

documents.abstract: This study aims to examine and analyze the effects of individual characteristics, job characteristics, and job placement on employee performance at the Election Supervisory Agency (Bawaslu) of West Sulawesi Province, both individually and simultaneously. The study employs a quantitative method with an associative research approach. The population consists of 43 employees, all of whom were included as respondents using a saturated sampling technique. Data were collected through questionnaires, observations, interviews, and documentation. Instrument quality was assessed through validity and reliability tests, while the data were analyzed using classical assumption tests and multiple linear regression analysis with the assistance of SPSS software. Hypotheses were tested using t-tests, an F-test, and the coefficient of determination. The findings indicate that (1) individual characteristics have a positive and statistically significant effect on employee performance; (2) job characteristics have a positive and statistically significant effect on employee performance; (3) job placement has a positive and statistically significant effect on employee performance; and (4) individual characteristics, job characteristics, and job placement jointly have a statistically significant effect on employee performance. Individual characteristics emerged as the strongest predictor, with a standardized beta coefficient of 0.626. The adjusted R-squared value of 0.753 indicates that the three independent variables collectively explain approximately 75.3% of the variation in employee performance, while the remaining variation is not explained by the model. These findings highlight the importance of employee competencies, effective job design, and appropriate job placement in improving employee performance within public sector institutions.

In modern times, artificial intelligence (AI) is considered one of the most important technological revolutions in the industrialization process. Artificial Intelligence technologies are widely used to digitize, automate, and increase the efficiency of production. The basis of the “Industry 4.0” concept is precisely artificial intelligence, big data, robotics, and internet technologies. In this regard, studying the applications of Artificial Intelligence in the industrial field is relevant both theoretically and practically. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming various industries by providing new solutions, increasing efficiency, and reducing costs. Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the development of computer systems that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, problem solving, perception, decision making, and language understanding. Artificial Intelligence systems use various techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision to analyze large amounts of data and make predictions or decisions based on that analysis. Some examples of AI applications include virtual personal assistants, self-driving cars, image and speech recognition, and medical diagnostics and treatment. AI is a rapidly developing field and can transform many industries and aspects of daily life. Applications of AI in the industrial field are accompanied by automation of production, energy saving, increased safety, and the creation of new technological capabilities. In the future, the competitiveness of industrial enterprises will be measured precisely by the level of use of AI technologies.

documents.abstract: Background and objective: Nursing faculty have been hesitant to incorporate artificial intelligence into coursework due to various reasons, including the risk of affecting academic integrity and the potential for receiving inaccurate information. As nursing cohorts continue to grow, innovative approaches are needed to meet learning objectives; such as artificial intelligence. Incorporating artificial intelligence into group projects may increase responsible, ethical, and critical use of artificial intelligence and support programs in managing larger cohorts. The purpose of this initiative was to integrate artificial intelligence into the literature review process for a quality improvement group project to develop students’ ability to use artificial intelligence responsibly, ethically, and critically. This approach included validating the accuracy of artificial intelligence generated information. Methods: This initiative was offered as an honors conversion opportunity within the Clinical Science II course to undergraduate nursing students. Six students opted to participate and were divided into two groups of three. Groups selected a topic related to the course content and aligned it with one of the Joint Commission national patient safety goals. Groups developed a clinical question, search strategy, conducted a literature review, and used artificial intelligence to identify evidence. Results: Benefits of using artificial intelligence included the generation of creative ideas, provision of workflow steps, and a broad range of solutions. Challenges included a lack of concrete examples and a tendency for artificial intelligence generated information to be more practical than theoretical. Groups found artificial intelligence generated findings aligned with most articles from their literature reviews. Conclusions: Incorporating the utilization of artificial intelligence into nursing curriculums can help programs monitor usage while managing growing cohorts. Allowing students to engage with artificial intelligence under guided instruction enhances understanding of its practical applications in clinical settings. This will better prepare students for real-world practice while ensuring academic integrity is maintained.

documents.abstract: Virtual higher education seeks to address the growing demand for sustainable, inclusive, and ethical educational models within the context of digital transformation and the progressive integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The purpose of this study is to analyze the pedagogical, ethical, and organizational conditions required for the implementation of AI applications related to academic tutoring and student monitoring from the perspective of educational sustainability. The research adopts a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design. The quantitative phase consists of a questionnaire using Likert-scale items administered to students, faculty members, and academic tutors, followed by a qualitative phase based on semi-structured interviews aimed at exploring in greater depth the perceptions, experiences, and tensions identified during the quantitative stage. The discussion is structured around four key dimensions: institutional ethical governance, AI-supported academic tutoring, digital inclusion, and systematic evaluation. The findings suggest that AI can contribute to ensuring the continuity of students’ educational pathways, enhancing personalized learning experiences, and enabling the early identification of academic risks. However, it may also give rise to challenges related to privacy, algorithmic bias, surveillance, technological dependency, and the displacement of professional judgment. The study concludes that AI can effectively contribute to educational sustainability only if it is implemented as a transparent decision-support tool that complements, rather than replaces, human judgment while ensuring data protection, accessibility, faculty oversight, and institutional accountability.

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon. We investigate whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior interactions and leverage them to improve future negotiation outcomes. We introduce a repeated, multi-party, multi-issue negotiation framework in which recurring agents participate in a sequence of negotiation games while one participant covertly attempts to prevent agreement. After each game, agents assess their counterparts and maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over to subsequent negotiations. We compare trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents and analyze how explicit trust influences negotiation outcomes. Our results reveal a \emph{trust--agreement gap}: trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games, but accurate trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements. Trust increases agreement rates by up to 23 percentage points, but only when agents are explicitly guided to use it in their decisions. Explicit trust can therefore improve repeated LLM negotiations, but its value depends critically on how trust is assessed and incorporated into agents' reasoning.

University classrooms are where students acquire higher-level knowledge and develop skills for future professional development in a work environment that requires decision-making through analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. Artificial intelligence provides guidance to students as a support tool, but there is a risk that it may become invasive or substitute for solving, thinking, and dictating what should or can be done, resulting in negative impacts and generating significant risks. The objective is to investigate students' reflections of artificial intelligence for their proper training, which must consciously consider sustainability and the importance of the philosophy of science to position it as a technological advancement. The paradigm is qualitative, as it involves discussion and the speculative aspects of the philosophy of science. Worksheets and a Likert scale were used to collect information. The results show that approximately 35% of respondents agree on the positive and negative aspects of its use, highlighting risks and benefits. The most radical position, which defends artificial intelligence, is held by a very small percentage of the total respondents.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing project work while raising questions about how project professionals acquire and demonstrate competence. This article develops an evidence-informed framework for learning and educating project managers in AI-enabled environments. It undertakes a focused integrative analysis of findings from a 2026 survey of 300 German project professionals and selected empirical studies of AI-assisted project work, learning, and education. In the source survey, 91% reported readiness to develop competences, learning-by-doing was the most highly rated individual format, and mentoring/coaching was the highest-rated organizational support measure. Experimental and classroom evidence indicates that AI can improve task performance and provide instructional scaffolding, but output improvements do not necessarily imply durable learning or sound contextual judgment. We propose a three-part educational architecture encompassing foundational project management judgment, responsible human–AI collaboration, and project value-oriented orchestration. It is operationalized through scaffolded practice, explicit AI-use rules, progressively independent assessments, and workplace-supported development. The framework is a conceptual synthesis, not an intervention validated by the source survey. The article offers testable propositions and an evaluation agenda for universities, employers, trainers, and professional associations.

documents.abstract: The application of artificial intelligence (AI) to education and policy-making offers them both hotly awaited possibilities and urgent ethical concerns. This conceptual paper, aims to understand how ethical AI models can drive data-informed decision-making that is in line with sustainability missions, ethical research practices and procedures. Though AI holds untapped tools for analyzing complex data, introducing prognosatory potential, and assisting policy creation, the paper negates that unchecked use might actually perpetuate biases, and foster irresponsibility and loss of transparency which will weakenedsocieties..A conceptual framework is developed in the paper that situates ethical AI as a connecting point between raw data and actionable decisions in the subject area of policy and research education. Using cutting-edge paradigms from data sciences, sustainability studies and educational literature: The pillars of the framework are four: (1) fairness and accountability of algorithmic models; (2) inclusion in data representations with stakeholders; (3) transparency in decision-making; and (4) outcomes towards sustainability for long-term social and ecological welfare..By incorporating these pillars into both policy and research education, the research identifies how institutions could guide their future African leaders and researchers to provide them with the competences to think critically with AI while ensuring ethical protection. The paper is further used to show how the adoption of ethical AI improves the legitimacy of evidence-based policymaking and is used to support changes in educational practices aimed on instilling responsibility through innovation. Informatics Research: This study adds to the ongoing discussion on the governance of AI, by presenting design frameworks based on education and policy that embedding ethics in the design of data-driven system itself. Ultimately, the study calls for human-centered approach to AI, which not only helps make decisions faster but also ensures that the technological advancements are on the path for sustainable and socially responsible futures.

documents.abstract: Abstract Computational or machine ethics examines how morality could be implemented in machines and represented computationally. In the cognitive sciences, different architectures (rule-based and connectionist) have been proposed. Nevertheless, such approaches have limitations when incorporating ethical claims. With the rise of artificial intelligence, new ways of simulating moral expertise seem possible, where chatbots can serve as dialogue partners for moral orientation. However, as I will argue, such systems lack a theoretical grounding in metaethics, as do the former approaches. In order to align such systems ethically and ground them conceptually, a topography of moral competence must be developed. By outlining this topography, I will show some directions for further research and how such systems might enhance us morally.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure led to runaway cascades that generated extreme and unpredictable collective recommendations increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. Compared to humans, LLM populations were generally far more susceptible to herding behavior, and unlike humans, LLM cascades were less able to self-correct. This vulnerability has implications for multi-agent collaboration in recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is widely framed as democratizing skilled work by lowering the barrier to producing professional output. Drawing on 21 semi-structured interviews with 27 workers across 21 small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) in Kenya and Nigeria (July to October 2023), we find that availability alone did not make participation workable. In participants' accounts, drafting was rarely the hard part. The consequential work was making AI-assisted drafts defensible enough to circulate to clients. We identify five intertwined practices through which participants made generative AI workable: using it as draft labour, steering outputs through iterative interaction, switching and comparing across tools, performing release work to make outputs accountable before circulation, and repairing context misfit when outputs failed local requirements. We make two central contributions. First, we specify release work as a distinct, boundary-facing form of accountability labour, evidenced through verification gates, traceability reconstruction when sources fail, and non-delegation boundaries that decide what can ship. Second, we show how localization and representational failures, which we call context misfit, operate in everyday work as a recurring breakdown-and-repair class, including failures of local language, institutional knowledge, and the credible representation of African people and places, and we document the repair repertoire they demanded. Reframing democratization as workable participation, we argue that reported gains were conditional on this accountability and repair labour, and we translate the findings into four design directions for workplace generative AI. We treat Kenya and Nigeria as two situated cases, not as a representative sample of SMBs or the Global South.

documents.abstract: The use of Conversational Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is growing as a way to interact with health information, especially for the public. This theory-based conceptual synthesis suggests a multilevel governance approach to reducing the likelihood for generated information to become unsafe action – GenAI health information resilience (GenAI-HIR). Its contribution is immediately usable and practical — deploying organizations and public-health actors and public-health actors can use the consequence-based control tiers, actor-specific safeguards, and domain-level audit anchors, and the proposed competency configuration still needs to be validated and is a research agenda for the future. Five conceptually distinct functions at the individual and workforce levels describe at which point protection may contribute to the decision pathway, but are not necessarily assumed to be empirically separable: recognize, interrogate, verify, contextualize, and escalate. Organizational capacity is limited to controls particular to created health information such as authorized sources, attainable human routing, incident monitoring and corrective action. Platform and regulatory conditions are constraints, safety, access, calibrated trust, and equity, outcomes. The framework was created using an expert guided purposive synthesis of the 62 sources that were retained, not a systematic review process. It distinguishes between an explanatory risk model and a normative control architecture and categorizes outputs with respect to type of output, severity, urgency, reversibility, context dependence, mitigation feasibility, and remaining risk. Falsification criteria are now included in six propositions. The candidate self-report indicators are kept as material for the cognitive interviewing only and must be correlated with behavioral vignettes before use for psychometric purposes. GenAI-HIR is therefore not a validated scale, certification standard or replacement for accessible professional care; it is a model for competency that can be falsified in future research and a governance structure that can be audited for current implementation.
