Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to transform clinical practice, but its adoption coincides with a longstanding decline in bedside medicine. Herein, we argue that reintroducing Oslerian principles into medical training may be essential to ensure that technological progress does not come at the expense of the physician-patient relationship. Throughout, we use the term AI to refer to tools built on algorithms, from risk calculators and predictive models to large language models, that produce predictions, classifications or recommendations. These tools have no agency of their own: they operate only on the data supplied to them, and their implementation depends on how clinicians and institutions design and deploy them.William Osler never saw an algorithm. He died in 1919, a century before "artificial intelligence" entered the clinical vocabulary. And yet no figure in the history of medicine is better equipped to tell us what we are about to lose 1 . Osler's central achievement was a discipline of the mind: the conviction that the practice of medicine must rest on direct observation of the patient and on the relationship between patient and physician. We argue that this discipline is now under direct threat, and that AI tools, as currently deployed, tend to hasten its erosion rather than reverse it -unless we act deliberately to stop it. In fact, the physician-patient relationship has already been reshaped by decades of patient access to medical information through the internet and social media. This shift has been amplified by the development of health-related AI tools, which increase patients' knowledge but also expose them to misinformation and misinterpretation. Nowadays, patients often arrive at the clinical encounter having already formed their own interpretations about their disease, which directly impacts the dialogue with the physician from the very first minutes of the encounter -a dynamic Osler never had to confront. Oslerian principles must therefore be adapted to this new reality, in which both physician and patient increasingly approach the clinical encounter already shaped by algorithms.Clarifying what AI can do -and will not do in the foreseeable future AI tools can go extraordinarily far in the medical process -synthesizing literature at a scale no human can match, flagging patterns in imaging and pathology that trained eyes miss, drafting notes, triaging risk, generating differential diagnoses, and suggesting therapeutic options in seconds. None of this is in serious dispute anymore, and clinicians who dismiss it outright are being unrealistic.On the other hand, it is illusory to imagine that AI will, in the foreseeable future, replace clinical observation and the personal relationship between doctor and patient. This needs to be said plainly, not hedged. Diagnosis by patternmatching on data is not the same as sitting at the bedside of anxious patients, watching how they behave, picking up on what they leave unsaid, and actually building the trust that makes adherence possible. Whatever level of performance AI models will achieve in the future, they will remain trained on the past, and no model can substitute for what happens, uniquely, in the present, between two people.There is also a more technical reason why bedside medicine remains indispensable: AI can only reason about the reality that has been captured and digitized. An algorithm implicitly assumes that what is absent from the record does not exist. Because important information reaches the record only if a physician observes it, an algorithm working from an incomplete record can return a seemingly precise but inaccurate output, creating an illusion of certainty. Oslerian observation is therefore not a nostalgic complement to AI but a technical prerequisite for its validity: no AI tool can compensate for a hurried or incomplete examination. Far from making clinical skills obsolete, AI demands sharper skills in listening, observation and physical examination.Losing the lessons learned at the bedside is not a hypothetical risk, nor is it a new one. For decades, medical departments have been organized around organ systems and specialized technologies. This process of specialization and subspecialization -a transformation that long predates the current wave of AI adoption -has produced remarkable diagnostic and therapeutic advances, but it has also fragmented the physician's view of the patient as a whole and made a holistic approach harder to sustain. Another powerful driver of this change has been the growth of administrative and documentation burden: in ambulatory practice, a time-and-motion study found that physicians spend nearly two hours on electronic health records and desk work for every hour of direct clinical face time with patients 2 , and administrative burden has been associated with lower intrinsic motivation among physicians and poorer patient-reported experience of care 3 .Consistent with this, studies among internal medicine trainees have documented a clear decline in direct time with patients for well over a decade 4 , and the trend is still underway today in several disciplines. For example, in hematologic malignancies, where AI-based tools are being rapidly adopted to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions 5 , physicians increasingly spend more time in offices in front of computer screens -reviewing algorithmic outputs, multiomic profiles, and risk calculators -often making therapeutic decisions before they examine the patient, so that the consultation risks becoming a confirmation of a decision already made elsewhere, rather than the encounter from which the decision should emerge. Deployed carelessly, AI tools are likely to deepen this pattern rather than correct it. Many current incentives push in that direction: institutions will reward the efficiency of deciding early, physicians will gravitate toward the workflow that is faster and less cognitively taxing, and the tools themselves are easiest to deploy on data that are already structured and available before the visit. Left to market and workflow pressures alone, AI is unlikely to restore the clinical encounter and may further hollow it out. This is the central danger. However, AI can also work in the opposite direction. In a recent randomized trial, ambient AI scribes, which transcribe the consultation and draft the clinical note, were associated with reduced physician burnout, and doctors reported that the technology allowed them to engage better with their patients 6 . Such tools can return the physician's attention from the screen to the patientprovided that the time they free is deliberately protected for the clinical encounter.This is precisely why Osler's teaching should not be treated as an outdated precept, but as the specific countermeasure this moment requires. We argue that it should be urgently reintroduced as a structural component of clinical education, integrated into, not appended to, the technical curriculum. Three Oslerian principles should anchor that effort: "Listen to the patient; he is telling you the diagnosis." What the physician personally learns at the patient's bedside should always come first -a principle physicians in subspecialty training are especially at risk of losing, as AI output can easily become the main input they consult before reaching a conclusion. AI output should inform that conclusion but not replace it."Medicine is learned by the bedside and not in the classroom." Osler's most consequential reform was moving medical education out of the lecture hall and to the patient's side. A century later, the direction of travel has reversed: trainees now often learn to interpret data before they learn to examine a patient. That sequence needs to be corrected, with protected, unhurried bedside time built into training and explicitly shielded from the pressure to consult the algorithm first. "Imperturbability." In his famous 1889 address, Aequanimitas 7 , Osler used this word to describe the calm and steady judgment a physician needs when facing suffering, urgency and clinical uncertainty. Applied to the output of AI, the same discipline must hold: neither adopting it blindly, a failure known as automation bias 8 , nor dismissing it out of hand, but checking it as rigorously as any other clinical evidence, including against what the physician has personally observed.These principles cannot be reintroduced as a simple return to an earlier era; they must be adapted to a clinical environment now shaped not only by AI but also by electronic health records, an ever-expanding volume of diagnostic data, and patients arriving informed -and sometimes misinformed. The task for training programs is not to teach learners to resist these developments but to integrate them without displacing direct observation and reasoning. Concretely, this could include bedside practice that requires trainees to form their own clinical impression before consulting AI output, case studies comparing bedside findings with AI-generated information, exercises showing how omissions in the history or examination alter an algorithm's output, and communication exercises on discussing AI- derived information with patients. These skills should be embedded into formal assessment and not treated as incidental.Discussions on "AI and the future of medicine" too often lead to wishful thinking that is very unlikely to be implemented. Instead, they should lead to concrete proposals, such as treating the clinical encounter as a parameter to be measured in academic medical centers. Time at the bedside is a necessary but insufficient indicator, since more time does not automatically translate into better care. We therefore propose mixed metrics combining the time physicians actually spend with patients, the diagnostic accuracy of the physician working with AI compared with either alone, and patients' perceptions of empathy and trust assessed with validated instruments such as the Consultation and Relational Empathy (CARE) measure 9 .William Osler would have welcomed the advent of AI in medicine, but he would have insisted that every AI tool be held to a single non-negotiable question: does it bring the physician closer to the patient, or does it interpose itself between them? On present evidence, in disciplines already reorganized around screens and algorithms, many AI deployments are failing that test 10 . The remedy is not to slow the technology down. It is to speed up, urgently, the reintroduction of Osler's principles into the training of every physician who will use it.

documents.abstract: Generative AI imposes new metacognitive demands on knowledge workers as their work shifts from production to planning, evaluation, and orchestration. In a randomized, between-subjects experiment on AI-assisted writing (297 workers, 594 essays), we test dynamically-generated metacognitive scaffolds supporting goal specification and task decomposition. We find that scaffolds improve writing quality, with this boost persisting in short-lag transfer when scaffolds are removed. We also find evidence of improved topic recall three days later. These effects are consistent with observed changes in how people learn to prompt AI systems after exposure to scaffolding. However, scaffolded participants rate the AI as less helpful and more cognitively demanding even as they perform better, suggesting that subjective ease can understate the value of support. Our findings make the case for metacognitive scaffolds in AI-assisted knowledge work, revealing a productive friction worth designing for as workers increasingly delegate work to agentic AI.

The aim of the article is to reconstruct the lay conceptions held by students of early childhood and pre-primary education regarding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and its potential role in education. The study is grounded in the constructivist-interpretive paradigm, adopting an understanding of learning as a process of active construction and negotiation of meanings. The empirical material was collected using a questionnaire consisting of open, exploratory questions. The participants were students who had already completed coursework related to didactics but had not yet taken courses on modern technologies. A non-probability purposive sampling strategy was applied. The collected data were analyzed using interpretative thematic analysis. The results reveal tension in students’ common understandings of GenAI. On the one hand, GenAI is perceived as a tool that increases teacher effectiveness and facilitates access to information. On the other hand, the same feature raises concerns about limiting students’ cognitive independence. The results further suggest that future teachers’ ways of thinking about GenAI may be closely related to their understanding of the nature of learning and educational culture. Therefore, the study highlights the need to incorporate reflection on GenAI into teacher education – not as a technical issue, but as a didactic one.

documents.abstract: Abstract Negative feedback is essential for improvement but often elicits withdrawal instead of change. Adopting a micro-process perspective, this study examines the immediate affective, cognitive, and motivational responses that shape recipients’ engagement. Drawing on PSI theory, we challenge the predominantly negative view of negative affect and rumination by proposing immediate negative affect as catalyst for engagement and task-focused rumination as functional cognitive engagement. We also explored mindfulness as potential moderator. In a 2 x 2 online experiment ( N = 422), participants received personalized feedback using an innovative vignette paradigm. Moderated mediation analyses revealed a dual-pathway mechanism: Negative feedback directly reduced engagement while simultaneously promoting engagement indirectly. The mindfulness induction did not moderate affect or feedback responses (task-focused rumination, intention to adapt behavior). These findings highlight negative feedback’s complexity, demonstrating that it can evoke both withdrawal and engagement. Future longitudinal research should examine the full improvement process and longer mindfulness interventions.

documents.abstract: This qualitative study examined how secondary school English teachers in Philippine public schools negotiate and reconstruct pedagogy in response to artificial intelligence (AI). Using Constructivist Grounded Theory, the study drew on intensive semi-structured interviews with seven English teachers from selected public secondary schools under the Schools Division Office of Batangas City. Initial and focused coding, constant comparison, memo writing, and theoretical integration generated seven interrelated categories: continually recalibrating pedagogical practice; protecting the learning work from technological substitution; reconstructing assessment to make learning and authorship visible; negotiating ethical boundaries through contextual professional judgment; building adaptive capacity through collegial and institutional support; cultivating critical AI literacy while preserving human voice and communication; and mediating AI access to preserve equity and inclusive participation. Findings indicate that responsible adaptation involves recursive, context-sensitive professional judgment. Teachers evaluated whether AI supported intended competencies, preserved valid assessment and authorship, maintained ethical safeguards, and enabled equitable participation. The categories informed the emergent AI-Responsive English Pedagogy Framework. The study concludes that responsible integration requires bounded technological augmentation, professional learning, flexible institutional guidance, assessment redesign, and protection of authentic language learning.

This working paper presents Neuroforge Interactive Learning V1, a reproducible pilot study of rule identification through binary success/failure feedback. The experiment evaluates a symbolic learning agent against a fixed, non-learning baseline across 100 seeded episodes, with 16 actions per episode (1,600 actions per policy). The fixed baseline achieved 25.50% action accuracy (408/1,600), while the feedback-learning agent achieved 91.94% (1,471/1,600). All four automated tests passed in the local evaluation. The learner identifies an active rule from four predefined candidates using feedback. Its memory resets between episodes. The experiment does not establish neural-network learning, general artificial intelligence, autonomous discovery of arbitrary rules, or transfer to previously unseen rule families. The paper documents the experimental setup, observed results, limitations, and proposed future work toward interactive rule discovery and cross-task generalization. This is an independently authored, non-peer-reviewed research working paper associated with QuantEdge AI LLC.

This article examines the motivational, individual psychological, social, and organizational-pedagogical factors influencing the development of students' intellectual abilities through metacognitive strategies. A total of 280 students from the 7th and 9th grades participated in the study. The Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), developed by P.R. Pintrich, A.F. Smith, T. Garcia, and W.J. McKeachie, along with H. Gardner's Multiple Intelligences assessment method, was used to investigate correlations between motivational factors and different types of intelligence. The findings revealed positive correlations between intrinsic goal orientation, task value, self-efficacy for learning performance, elaboration, critical thinking, and metacognitive self-regulation and linguistic, logical-mathematical, and personal intelligences. Furthermore, the study highlights the significance of students' age-related characteristics, independent thinking, reflective abilities, and the educational environment in the application of metacognitive strategies. The findings substantiate the importance of psychological and pedagogical approaches aimed at strengthening intrinsic motivation, improving self-monitoring, and enhancing reflective activities to promote the development of students' intellectual potential.

Public officials perform diverse administrative, public-facing, emergency, and safety–critical tasks, yet their occupational risk profiles have rarely been characterized across actual job functions. In Korea, public officials have historically remained partly outside core occupational safety and health requirements, and systematic evidence on their occupational risk profiles across diverse job functions has been limited. This study applied the Public Officials’ Occupational Risk Assessment (PORA) tool to 36,779 Korean public officials to screen perceived occupational risks and identify occupation- and job-function-specific high-risk patterns. Respondents assessed exposure frequency and intensity for 24 occupational risk factors across psychological, organizational, ergonomic, physical, chemical, and biological domains. Risk scores were calculated as the product of frequency and intensity, and high-risk responses were defined as “high” or “very high” according to the PORA risk matrix. Prolonged sitting showed the highest mean risk score and high-risk prevalence, followed by public-facing work, fast work pace, time pressure, emotional stress, awkward posture, and repetitive upper-limb work. Frequency–intensity comparisons showed that some risks were driven by frequent exposure, whereas event-based psychological hazards received lower time-proportion-based frequency ratings but relatively higher intensity ratings. Occupation-specific logistic regression showed distinct profiles: general service officials were characterized by prolonged sitting and time pressure, police officers by broad psychological, ergonomic, and physical hazards, and firefighters by physical, chemical, biological, and emergency-response-related hazards. Job-function heatmaps and hierarchical clustering further revealed heterogeneous risk profiles across 22 main job functions. These findings highlight the need for job-function-based, participatory, and risk-prioritized occupational safety and health management in public organizations.

documents.abstract: On 1 May 2026, six Five Eyes cybersecurity agencies jointly issued Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services, the first coordinated Anglophone statement on the governance of LLM-based autonomous agents. This Comment argues that, although the Guidance offers competent cybersecurity risk management within its stated remit, its institutional weight invites a broader governance reading that the document cannot bear, and that five structural limitations then come into view. First, the cybersecurity doctrines on which it relies are necessary but insufficient for agentic systems, whose delegated authority, underspecified goals, and long-horizon autonomy strain the assumptions of conventional controls. Second, it privatises systemic risk by imposing duties on deployers without specifying public-law obligations, redress, or liability across the agentic value chain. Third, it prescribes human oversight without specifying the conditions of effective control, so that responsibility risks being assigned to reviewers who lack the information, authority, or time to exercise it. Fourth, it reduces accountability to auditability, confusing a technical property with a legal relation between duty-holders and affected parties. Fifth, the security-defined mandates of its six authoring agencies, and the intelligence-oversight structures within which most of them sit, raise questions of institutional voice, while its Five Eyes-only authorship raises a risk of divergence from the AI frameworks now emerging in the European Union, the Republic of Korea and Japan. The Comment concludes by outlining the elements of an enforceable, rights-protective, cross-jurisdictional legal regime that should supplement, rather than be displaced by, the technical controls the Guidance recommends.

documents.abstract: Background: Patient trust may determine whether artificial intelligence (AI) is accepted in dental care, particularly when AI contributes to diagnosis or treatment planning. We aimed to synthesize patient-reported trust, confidence, acceptance, and preferences regarding dental AI and to identify factors associated with these outcomes. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 2 June 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed with the revised JBI tool for analytical cross-sectional studies. Because outcomes and metrics were heterogeneous, findings were synthesized narratively. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261439049). Results: The final synthesis included eight studies comprising 3171 participants from five countries. Attitudes were generally favourable when AI supported rather than replaced dentists. In one study, 47.7% accepted AI-assisted interpretation of diagnostic data, whereas 10.8% trusted an entirely AI-generated diagnosis. Another study found that 84.9% supported AI analysis of dental images followed by dentist review. A fixed-order vignette study improved lesion recognition but did not significantly change trust in the dentist. Interpretation was limited by non-probability sampling, heterogeneous and often non-validated measures, incomplete control of confounding, and reporting inconsistencies. Conclusions: Available evidence suggests conditional acceptance of dental AI, particularly when dentists retain oversight. Confidence in the prevalence estimates of trust and acceptance is low; these findings do not establish that AI improves trust. More representative studies using validated, conceptually distinct outcome measures are required.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background: Research on teachers' AI use has largely focused on whether teachers use AI or how many purposes they report. These measures cannot show how teachers combine AI across different parts of instructional work or whether professional learning relates differently to those combinations. Objectives: This study identified patterns of professional AI use among lower-secondary teachers and examined whether AI-related professional learning differed across them. Methods: We analysed 2024 Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) data from 25,705 teachers in 54 education systems who reported using AI for teaching or student learning. Equal-system weighted latent class analysis examined eight purposes. Adjusted three-step models related AI-related professional learning to profile membership while accounting for classification uncertainty and teacher characteristics. Results and Conclusions: A four-profile solution was retained: preparation-focused (40.07%), design-and-adaptation-focused (23.87%), data-and-feedback-focused (18.70%), and broad-purpose use (17.37%). Beyond breadth, the two intermediate profiles covered a similar range of purposes but diverged in material adaptation and student-data review. Among professional-learning participants, AI-related rather than non-AI content was associated with higher odds of design-and-adaptation membership (OR = 2.03, 95% CI [1.62, 2.53]) and broad-purpose membership (OR = 2.40, 95% CI [1.99, 2.89]) relative to data-and-feedback membership; broad-purpose and design-and-adaptation membership did not differ significantly. Teacher AI use therefore varies in both breadth and instructional purpose. The findings move beyond overall prevalence and provide a task-based basis for designing and evaluating AI-related professional learning, while leaving its effects on teachers’ practice to be tested longitudinally. Manuscript status Under review at the Journal of Computer Assisted Learning. Registration timing This record documents a completed study. Data analysis and manuscript preparation were completed before this registration, and the manuscript is currently under journal review. This is a retrospective registration, not a prospective preregistration.

documents.abstract: This study was initiated by the uneven learning motivation among junior high school students in Coding and Artificial Intelligence (CAI) subjects. The research aims to enhance students’ learning motivation through a project-based gamification strategy. The method employed was Classroom Action Research (CAR) based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, conducted in two cycles with 31 students as subjects. The learning process implemented Project-Based Learning (PjBL) integrated with six gamification elements (clear goals, points, challenges, badges, feedback, and leaderboards) through a simple Scratch game development project. Data were collected using an adapted Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), observations, field notes, and documentation, and analyzed descriptively. The results showed an increase in students’ learning motivation, with the classical average rising from 3.06 (76.39%) in the pre-cycle to 3.24 (81.00%) in Cycle I and 3.38 (84.39%) in Cycle II, and all motivation aspects improving. Students reaching the minimum “High” criterion (score ≥ 3.00) increased from 51.61% (16 students) in the pre-cycle to 77.42% (24 students) in Cycle I, and reached the classical success target at 80.65% (25 students) in Cycle II. In Cycle II, a layered troubleshooting strategy using a Generative AI chatbot as a coding assistant, followed by peer feedback, appeared to support more persistent and independent problem-solving, although the gains were moderate and uneven across students, and self-regulation remained the lowest-scoring aspect (3.09). In conclusion, project-based gamification was accompanied by an increase in junior high school students’ learning motivation in CAI subjects.

Work-related stress is a leading occupational health concern, and a substantial literature suggests its consequences differ between women and men. Most of that literature, however, establishes that a difference exists without identifying the mechanism responsible. This study examined the physical and mental health consequences of work-related stress among employed women and men, and tested whether differences persisted after psychosocial working conditions were controlled. A comparative cross-sectional design was adopted. Data were collected from 101 full-time employees aged 25-50 in Bengaluru, India; the analytical sample comprised 100 participants (50 women, 50 men). A 50-item instrument assessed perceived stress, working conditions, physical symptoms, emotional wellbeing and coping. Physical health and emotional wellbeing scales showed good reliability (alpha = .83 and .86). Five of six hypotheses were unsupported: women and men did not differ in perceived stress (p = .584, d = -0.11), physical symptoms (p = .986, d = 0.004) or emotional wellbeing (p = .575, d = 0.11), and gender did not moderate the stress-health relationship. One significant difference emerged: men reported greater problem-focused coping (p < .001, d = -0.73), although the predicted difference in emotion-focused coping did not appear. Perceived stress correlated strongly with physical symptoms (r = .55) and emotional wellbeing (r = .62), explaining 30% and 39% of variance. Findings are consistent with a differential-exposure account: where working conditions were comparable, health consequences were comparable.

The expansion of Google digital services and the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence have intensified the importance of privacy, user control, and trust in digital-service relationships. This study examines whether privacy concern and perceived privacy control are associated with trust in Google digital services and whether these perceptions, together with trust, explain users’ intention to continue using Google/Gemini services in Bangladesh. Drawing on Privacy Calculus Theory and Trust Theory, the study develops a model in which privacy concern is expected to reduce trust, perceived privacy control is expected to strengthen trust, and trust is expected to increase continued-use intention. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was applied to the Group 2 Google master dataset. After screening, 385 complete cases were retained, with all retained respondents satisfying the attention-check criterion. Three-item measures captured privacy concern, perceived privacy control, trust, and continued-use intention using a five-point Likert scale. Composite-score regressions with bootstrap inference were used to reproduce the planned SEM/PLSSEM-oriented structural assessment. The results indicate that perceived privacy control positively predicts trust (β = .167, p = .001), whereas privacy concern does not have a statistically significant effect on trust (β = .080, p = .114). Trust is a substantial positive predictor of continued-use intention (β = .347, p < .001), and perceived privacy control also has a positive direct association with continued use (β = .129, p = .007). Privacy concern does not significantly predict continued use (β = .058, p = .217). Bootstrap mediation indicates a significant indirect effect of perceived privacy control through trust, while the privacy-concern indirect effect is not statistically distinguishable from zero. The findings suggest that users’ perceived ability to understand and manage privacy settings may be more consequential for trust and continued use than generalized privacy concern alone. The study contributes Bangladesh-specific evidence to privacy-calculus and trust research and offers practical implications for Google and other digital-service providers seeking to strengthen transparency, user control, and durable trust in the generative-AI era.

Psychological well-being at work has become a central topic in organizational and sport psychology because it bears on health, performance, and the sustainability of a career. Sports coaches work under heavy demands: large workloads, competitive pressure, and complex interpersonal relationships. Such conditions can affect their well-being, which in turn shapes how they coach, the decisions they make, and the outcomes they achieve. This chapter sets out the conceptual foundations of psychological well-being and considers their relevance to the coaching profession. It reviews the main theoretical models, including hedonic and eudaimonic approaches, and examines how job demands are balanced against personal resources, drawing on positive psychology, occupational health psychology, and sport psychology. It then synthesizes empirical work on stress, burnout, interpersonal relationships, and coping among coaches in order to identify the determinants and consequences of well-being in this profession. The chapter also points to the main gaps in the literature, in particular, how little empirical research addresses coaches specifically. It closes with recommendations for future research and for evidence-based interventions that can support sustainable psychological well-being among sports coaches.

Workplace ergonomics is a key component of occupational health, as it considers the interaction between the worker, job characteristics, and the physical environment. The aim of this study was to determine the relationship between ergonomic factors and the frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms among administrative employees of the Regional Government in Bluefields, SACCR, Nicaragua. A quantitative, observational, cross-sectional, and correlational study was conducted with a sample of 112 workers. A questionnaire was used to assess ergonomic factors and musculoskeletal symptoms, complemented by semi-structured observation of workstations and the physical work environment. Data were processed using IBM SPSS 26® software, employing descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square test, and Spearman's rho. Of the participants, 96 (85.7 %) reported musculoskeletal symptoms, with frequent and very frequent pain being the most common presentations. Unfavorable ergonomic conditions related to posture and the physical environment were identified. The frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms showed statistically significant associations with the perception of work postures (ρ = −0.359; p < 0.001), ambient noise (ρ = 0.283; p = 0.002), humidity (ρ = 0.235; p = 0.020), and ambient heat (ρ = 0.215; p = 0.023). The findings demonstrate that specific postural factors as well as those related to equipment and the physical work environment are associated with the frequency of musculoskeletal symptoms, underscoring the need to strengthen ergonomic interventions focused on workstation design, environmental conditions, and work organization.

documents.abstract: The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in learning mathematics among fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05. This study was motivated by the increasing use of generative AI as a learning tool and the low level of students’ interest in mathematics. A quantitative approach with a correlational survey design was employed. The population consisted of all fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05, and a saturated sampling technique was used. Data were collected primarily through questionnaires, with observations, documentation, and interviews serving as supporting data. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson Product-Moment correlation analysis. The results showed a strong positive relationship between the use of generative AI, represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in mathematics learning (r = 0.682, p < 0.001). This finding indicates that higher use of generative AI was associated with higher interest in mathematics learning among fifth-grade students. The findings suggest that the appropriate use of generative AI may provide teachers with complementary tools for creating more interactive mathematics learning experiences and may be considered in supporting students’ learning interest. The study provides practical implications for teachers in integrating AI-based learning tools appropriately as complementary resources in primary mathematics education.

documents.abstract: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly incorporated into journalistic work, raising questions concerning transparency, authorship, editorial responsibility, human verification, and organizational governance. This study examines reported transparency practices and professional perceptions concerning AI use among journalism professionals linked to media organizations and news-production environments in Ecuador. A mixed-methods design combined a non-probability online survey of 53 eligible professionals with seven semi-structured interviews involving six journalism professionals and one communication academic with professional experience in journalism. The quantitative component was analyzed descriptively, while the qualitative component was examined through a deductive and interpretive analysis structured around four predefined thematic domains. AI use was reported by 48 of the 53 survey participants (90.6%), with both instrumental and generative applications identified. Among applicable responses, 39.5% reported the existence of a specific AI-related deontological code, 59.2% reported having received instructions from superiors, and 29.3% reported an obligation to disclose AI use to audiences. Human verification was the most frequently selected component of proposed internal AI rules (79.2%). The interviews showed uneven levels of organizational formalization, including verbal instructions, emerging guidelines, and differing thresholds for disclosure, while consistently emphasizing human editorial judgment and responsibility. The findings indicate that transparency in AI-assisted journalism is multidimensional and unevenly institutionalized across the professional environments represented in the study. These results provide sample-bound evidence from Ecuador and should not be interpreted as a national estimate of media transparency.

documents.abstract: This article argues that trust in AI-mediated public services depends not only on whether systems are accurate, fair, or efficient, but on how their presence is made visible to the people affected by them. Across welfare, healthcare, and border governance, artificial intelligence increasingly shapes decisions about access, movement, support, and rights. Yet these systems often operate within familiar institutional procedures, making their role difficult to see, interpret, or challenge. The article develops the idea of AI visibility to explain how different forms of disclosure shape public trust. It distinguishes between invisible AI, partially visible AI, and fully disclosed AI, showing how each can produce different responses: misplaced confidence, confusion, suspicion, or informed challenge. By shifting attention from technical performance alone to the public experience of decision-making, the article shows that trust is shaped by whether people can understand where authority lies and how decisions are made. Foregrounding visibility helps reframe debates on algorithmic governance, institutional legitimacy, and accountability. In an increasingly automated state, the question is not only whether AI systems can be trusted, but whether their role in public decisions can be meaningfully seen. Working paper (Version 1.0). This manuscript has not yet undergone peer review.

documents.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides opportunities for students to use technology as a tool to support self-reflection and emotional management. However, its use in the context of mental health requires an understanding of safety, ethics, privacy, and technological limitations. This community service program aimed to provide assistance to students in utilizing AI as a self-healing support tool in a safe, ethical, and responsible manner. The program was conducted at SMP Negeri 30 Muaro Jambi and involved 30 students and a school guidance and counseling teacher as a partner. The program employed a Participatory Action Research (PAR) approach through four stages: preparation, core implementation, evaluation, and sustainability. The activities included orientation and initial assessment, emotion and stress recognition, overthinking management, self-healing techniques, AI-assisted self-reflection, and education on the ethics and safety of AI use. Participant responses were evaluated among 24 students using a 1–4 scale instrument covering material comprehension, usefulness, delivery, media, comfort, application of knowledge, and interest in future activities. The evaluation results showed an overall mean score of 3.43 out of 4.00, equivalent to 85.74%, which was categorized as very good. The highest score was found in participants' interest in attending similar activities in the future (90.91%), while all evaluation indicators remained in the very good category. The program indicates that practice-based assistance can help students understand AI as a support tool for self-reflection while strengthening their awareness of privacy, safety, ethics, and the limitations of AI in the context of mental health. Program sustainability is directed toward integrating the materials into school guidance and counseling services and continuing support through the school guidance and counseling teacher.

documents.abstract: As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly embedded in educational systems, yet their implications for self-regulated learning (SRL) and metacognitive development remain only partially understood. This study conducts a systematic literature review of 34 empirical and review articles investigating AI-driven learning analytics in formal education settings, focusing on their impact on SRL, motivation, and academic performance. Following PRISMA-aligned procedures, the review identifies studies involving AI-based analytics tools, standardized SRL or metacognitive assessments, and empirical designs with pre–post or comparison data. The results indicate that AI-driven systems such as predictive models, adaptive platforms, chatbots, and generative AI can strengthen core SRL processes, increase motivation and engagement, and improve academic outcomes across diverse subjects and educational levels. However, the review also reveals persistent implementation challenges, including infrastructural limitations, teacher preparedness, privacy and ethical issues, and potential over-reliance on AI that may weaken independent strategic thinking. The article concludes that AI-driven learning analytics can meaningfully support SRL when embedded within coherent pedagogical frameworks and supported by institutional policies, and it outlines directions for future research on mechanisms, equity, and long-term effects.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: People prefer deliberation to intuition, when judging how others solve hard problems, and they extend this to artificial agents. Yet in the moral domain, the preference may reverse as intuitive moral responses appear to signal good character. One explanation is that fast, intuitive responses show real emotional engagement. Since machines are thought to lack emotion, it is unclear whether a preference for intuition in the moral domain extends to AI. Across three preregistered studies (N = 2,173), we find that it does, but that it appears to be driven by commitment to moral norms and precedents rather than emotion. In Study 1, participants preferred intuitive reasoning for moral decisions and systematic reasoning for non-moral decisions, for human and AI agents alike. Intuitive moral reasoning signalled better character but was not clearly expected to produce better outcomes. In Study 2, the character preference persisted when the AI was described as being incapable of emotion. In Study 3, we held the decision fixed and varied how firmly the agent held the relevant moral norm. An agent who would never reconsider applying a moral norm was rated above one who would reconsider given sufficiently high stakes; and both above one who weighed costs and benefits case by case. Commitment raised character ratings more than expected-outcome ratings. The character-based cost of moral deliberation appears to be a cost of treating a moral norm as negotiable, and we found strong evidence that people apply this inference to machines and people alike.
topics: Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: Online learning platforms provide access to educational content, but many systems deliver the same material to every learner andoffer limited support for identifying individual learning needs. This paper proposes a Smart E-Learning Platform using ArtificialIntelligence (AI) that aims to personalize learning through learner profiles, progress tracking, recommendation methods,automated practice feedback, and a dashboard for learners and instructors. The proposed workflow collects learning activity andassessment results, processes relevant learning indicators, and recommends suitable resources or practice activities. Possible AImethods include rule-based recommendation as a baseline, content-based filtering, and supervised models when sufficientlabelled data is available. The platform is designed as an academic prototype and should be evaluated using measurableindicators such as recommendation relevance, task completion, learner satisfaction, and usability. No implementation results orimprovement percentages are claimed in this proposal. Privacy, transparency, accessibility, and instructor oversight areimportant requirements. The system is intended to support teaching and learning, not to replace teachers or make high-stakesdecisions about students
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The advent and rapid spread of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Generative Artificial Intelligencesystems have marked an epistemological and structural discontinuity in the Information Society.While the early phases of the digital transition were characterized by processes of digitization, indexing,and heuristic data retrieval — where the machine acted primarily as an archivist or intermediary towardprimary content —, the current configuration of algorithmic architecture responds to a qualitativelydifferent dynamic. Artificial Intelligence does not merely organize human knowledge; to function,learn its semantic structures, and provide real-time synthesis, it requires the continuous, massive, andsystematic assimilation of informational material produced by humanity.To describe this phenomenon of insatiable and structural nourishment, we propose here the analyticalcategory of «infofagia» (derived from the Greek root phagêin, "to eat", combined with the informationalprefix). AI infofagia does not constitute a mere computational phase of the machine — the technicalphase of training on datasets —, but rather a total sociological and psychological fact. It identifies anextractive and metabolic process in which humanity's entire cultural, scientific, artistic, andconversational production is converted into raw matter, "ingested" by mathematical models, digested,and finally returned in the form of synthetic and normalized output.Adopting the paradigm of infofagia allows us to overcome both purely deterministic readings oftechnology and apologetic visions tied to the alleged democratization of knowledge. Through theanalysis of empirical data, international case studies, and clinical-social feedback, this essaydemonstrates how the informational appetite of large algorithmic models is not neutral, but directlyretroacts upon economic structures, cultural diversity, and the psyche of the final consumer.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is collapsing the historical separation between statecraft and warcraft. This third volume of the series on Sovereign AI in the developing Global South examines how algorithmic systems are restructuring state authority in domestic governance and armed conflict. It first analyses "algorithmic statecraft": biometric digital public infrastructure and the risk of function creep, with India's Aadhaar and Kenya's Huduma Namba as cases, and predictive policing as a form of actuarial justice that can codify structural discrimination. The article then turns to "algorithmic warcraft": AI decision support systems used for target generation in Gaza, automation bias and the "triage trap" that hollow out meaningful human control, and bias in military AI. It traces the democratisation of lethality through commercial and AI-enabled drones in Myanmar, Sudan, Libya and the Sahel, Bangladesh's border-security modernisation in response to regional spillover, and generative AI as an instrument of cognitive warfare. It closes with the fractured diplomacy of the Global South in the UN Group of Governmental Experts on lethal autonomous weapons systems, and argues that sovereign resilience requires contextualised AI frameworks under strict civilian oversight together with a coordinated push for binding international norms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: While the practice of managing products to be delivered by means of large language models is growing rapidly and spreading, increasingly a new practitioner discourse is spreading in the field of product management. The PRD (Product Requirements Document), that for decades has been the core specification artifact of the function, would be replaced by the evaluation suite: a set of test cases scored by the evaluation environment of the product under development, the suite encoding in executable form what acceptable system behavior looks like. This simple statement is now almost a mantra in the practice of managing products, and so far has not been subject of any in-depth conceptual investigation. In the requirements engineering community for machine-learning-enabled systems, the challenges of specifying such systems have been analyzed in great detail, but this does not yet translate into practical artifacts and practices of requirements engineering that would be used by practitioners in industry. This paper attempts to specify in detail what is actually being replaced by the evaluation suite, and what corresponding problems and challenges are not addressed by the new artifact. The study is of a theoretical nature and builds on two streams of literature: requirements engineering for machine-learning-enabled systems, and measurement validity in artificial intelligence evaluation. First, we clarify that the PRD serves three separate purposes: defining requirements, coordinating stakeholders, and facilitating deliberation about product intent. We then argue that only the first of these functions is actually transferred to the evaluation suite. Next, we introduce the concept of specification residue, i.e. the portion of what has been specified that cannot be encoded in an executable form and therefore ends up in the black box of individual judgment. We identify three types of such residue. Finally, we introduce a contingency framework that specifies under which conditions of outcome measurability and process-constraint density eval-primary specification is appropriate. Our results indicate that executable specification may shift but not reduce the need for human product judgment, and, most importantly, that it removes the key artifact through which such judgment was previously recorded and contested.

This study investigated students’ engagement in Extensive Reading activities among English Education students at the University of Mataram. It aimed to describe students’ behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement and to identify the factors influencing their engagement. Although previous studies have reported the benefits of Extensive Reading for language proficiency and motivation, relatively little research has simultaneously examined the three engagement dimensions and their contextual influences in Indonesian EFL higher education. A qualitative descriptive design was employed with ten students completing a questionnaire and five students participating in semi-structured interviews. The closed-ended questionnaire functioned only as descriptive supporting data, while the semi-structured interviews provided the main qualitative explanations; therefore, the study was not designed as mixed methods and did not use inferential statistics. The questionnaire was used to identify general patterns through descriptive frequencies and percentages, while the interviews provided more detailed explanations of students’ reading experiences. The findings showed generally positive engagement. Behavioral engagement was reflected in relatively strong participation and effort, although reading consistency remained the main challenge. Emotional engagement was shown through interest, enjoyment, motivation, and positive attitudes toward English reading. Cognitive engagement appeared through reading strategies, comprehension monitoring, reflection, and connections between texts and prior knowledge. Five factors influenced engagement: reading materials and personal interest, language difficulty, time and academic responsibilities, motivation and academic requirements, and reading autonomy and lecturer support. Overall, students’ engagement in Extensive Reading was shaped by interacting personal, textual, and academic conditions.

Abstract Background Cognitive workload can influence performance and physiological responses during computer-based work, but these responses remain insufficiently understood in individuals with chronic non-specific low back pain (CNSLBP). This study investigated subjective, behavioral, electromyographic, and cardiac responses to increasing cognitive workload in individuals with CNSLBP and healthy controls during a dual-task computer-based paradigm. Methods Thirty participants, including 15 individuals with CNSLBP and 15 healthy controls, completed four experimental conditions combining two typing-speed levels and two cognitive workload levels. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). Behavioral performance and typing errors were recorded, while physiological responses were assessed using facial electromyography (EMG) and heart rate. Outcomes were analyzed using mixed repeated-measures analysis of variance to examine the effects of experimental condition, group, and their interaction. Results Increasing task demands significantly increased perceived workload (F = 34.63, p < 0.001) and reduced behavioral performance (F = 31.12, p < 0.001), whereas typing errors did not change significantly. No significant between-group differences were observed in perceived workload or behavioral performance. In contrast, participants with CNSLBP exhibited significantly greater RMS activity in the corrugator supercilii and frontalis muscles (both p < 0.001), and a significant condition × group interaction was observed for corrugator RMS (p = 0.018). Heart rate did not differ significantly across experimental conditions or between groups. Conclusions Individuals with CNSLBP maintained subjective workload ratings and behavioral performance comparable to healthy controls but exhibited greater facial muscle activation during task performance. These findings suggest that maintaining performance under cognitive demands may require greater physiological effort in individuals with CNSLBP. Multimodal assessment combining subjective, behavioral, and physiological measures may provide a more comprehensive understanding of cognitive workload responses in people with chronic low back pain.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human societies. In the many attempts to capture the novel trend of AI entering in all aspects of human life these days, hardly any research covers sustainability aspects of AI encroaching society. In the teaching of sustainability, AI appears as an way to improve carbon footprint as for energy savings opportunities – for instance by using online resources instead of physical books, reducing cognitive load of tedious tasks that had to be performed in educational settings previously, such as sifting through many books to find applicable cases in law school etc. At the same time, AI may create enormous environmental costs – e.g., through its electricity consumption use for big data storage and analytics – but also sustainability challenges – e.g., through eternally-living algorithms and technical devices. This chapter proposes weighing the costs and benefits of AI in sustainability education. In a Law & Economics analysis, the advantages and disadvantages of AI in sustainability education will be compared in order to present a framework to harvest the benefits but prepare for coping with the downsides of AI in sustainability education. Future student learning experience enhancement and educational changes due to AI in the future will be prospectively anticipated in the discussion. The future of education may positively develop in less cognitive load and diligent learning-by-heart but shift towards creative solution finding, navigating through a digital online jungle and development social network skills to find the right tools in a growing ocean of mushrooming AI advancements.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Purpose This study examines how the sustainability of learning at work varies within the same organisational context. The objective is to enhance understanding of sustainable learning at work by identifying learner typologies that demonstrate the diverse manifestations of workplace learning sustainability. Design The study draws on semi-structured interviews (n = 27) conducted with employees and managers in a Finnish ICT organisation. The concept of workplace learning is approached from a sociocultural perspective, with sustainable learning understood as continuous competence development supported by adequate resources, social interaction and opportunities to anticipate future learning needs. The data were analysed using a two-stage process combining thematic analysis and typification. Findings The analysis identified three distinct learner types: enthusiastic learners, exhausted learners and uncertain learners. The learner types exhibited variation across three dimensions of sustainable learning: knowledge sharing and interaction, management support, and anticipation of learning needs. Enthusiastic learners experienced learning as meaningful and manageable, indicating that sustainable learning was largely achieved. Among exhausted learners, sustainability was challenged by excessive workload and learning demands. For uncertain learners, sustainability was challenged by insecurity, limited participation in knowledge-sharing practices and difficulties in directing their competence development. Originality/value The study contributes to the research on sustainable learning at work by demonstrating how the sustainability of workplace learning varies between individuals even within the same organisational context. The findings highlight the importance of learning support, the affordances present within the workplace, and the role of employee agency in the process of shaping sustainable learning within the professional environment.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: The article substantiates theoretical and pedagogical foundations for developing students’ positive attitudes towards inclusive education and professional motivation. It explains the interrelationship of inclusive awareness, value acceptance, empathy, professional self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, practical experience and reflection. A staged methodology based on cases, simulations, service learning, microteaching and reflective portfolios is proposed.
topics: Inclusion and Disability in Education and Sport

documents.abstract: Teachers’ occupational well-being is associated with their capacity to sustain effective teaching and support students’ academic engagement. This study aimed to determine teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement in select districts of Cagayan de Oro City Division during the School Year 2026–2027. The study described the respondents’ profiles, assessed their occupational well-being and student engagement, examined the relationships between these variables, and tested the moderating effect of the respondents’ profiles. It used a quantitative descriptive-correlational design involving two hundred and twenty (220) Grade 7 public secondary school teachers selected through universal sampling. Data were collected using a modified questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson Correlation, and multiple regression. Findings showed that job satisfaction was stronger than work-life balance, while workload stress was more pronounced than burnout. Emotional engagement emerged as the strongest dimension of students’ academic engagement. Job satisfaction and work-life balance were significantly related to student engagement. Workload stress showed no significant relationship, while burnout had a weak link only to emotional engagement. Class size and teaching experience affected these relationships, but the subject taught did not. The study concludes that teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement are interconnected, although their relationships vary across specific dimensions and profile characteristics. School administrators and teachers are encouraged to strengthen work-life balance, manage workload stress and burnout, promote cognitive engagement, and provide support responsive to class size and teaching experience.

The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Capture-the-flag (CTF) competitions are used across the security community to recruit talent, build skills and sustain a competitive culture. As AI agents increasingly solve CTF challenges, three positions have emerged: that the format is obsolete, that it should become a benchmark for human-AI collaboration, and that headline claims overstate what the saturation of introductory benchmarks shows. This debate has been driven mainly by capability benchmarks, while the views of those who design, run and play CTFs remain largely unexamined. We report an exploratory qualitative study based on six interviews (seven participants) and eleven anonymous written responses from experienced CTF organisers and players. We interpret their accounts using Bourdieu's concepts of field and capital, and, for learning, the notion of threshold concepts. Participants did not offer a single verdict. Some were strongly critical of AI-assisted solving in competition; others wanted AI to be embraced and built into CTFs; still others took positions that depended on context. Strongly critical positions were voiced more often in anonymous written responses, a reminder that such positions are situated in the circumstances in which accounts are given. Participants involved in competition-focused CTFs described rankings that increasingly reflect access to AI models and money, and a loss of the satisfaction that made competing worthwhile. From an educational perspective, participants described students who solved challenges quickly but could not explain how they had done so. Participants disagreed about whether CTFs are preparation for real-world practice or a sport, and this seemed closely related to the stance they took. Many saw the enforcement of anti-AI measures as feasible only in on-site CTFs, and also largely dependent on trust. Several participants expressed doubt about CTF results still signalling individual skill levels to potential employers. We propose that this exploratory study into CTFs indicates a wider problem for the security workforce: when a measure of skill becomes cheap and easy to automate, a community must renegotiate what counts as legitimate performance. We also discuss implications for skills development, competition governance and hiring.

This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in improving students’ critical reading skills in higher education. As digital technologies increasingly shape learning environments, AI offers potential to enhance higher-order thinking. This research employed a quantitative approach using a quasi-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design. The participants were 30 sixth-semester students enrolled in the Qualitative Research on ELT course at Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa, selected through purposive sampling. The instrument was a standardized critical reading test measuring students’ ability to identify main ideas, analyze arguments, evaluate evidence, detect bias, and draw conclusions. It included multiple-choice and short-response items to assess analytical comprehension. The treatment integrated AI-based tools for text analysis, summarization, argument mapping, and reflective questioning. Students also compared their interpretations with AI-generated feedback to enhance metacognitive awareness. The intervention was conducted over four meetings under guided supervision. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and a paired-sample t-test. The findings revealed a statistically significant improvement in students’ posttest scores compared to pretest results at the 0.05 level. These results indicate that AI can effectively support critical reading development and foster deeper engagement with academic texts in EFL contexts.

This study examines the effects of transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards on job performance, with affective commitment serving as a mediating variable, in Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia. Public sector organizations face increasing demands to improve performance while maintaining bureaucratic accountability and regulatory compliance. Understanding the mechanisms that influence performance in such institutional settings is therefore essential. A quantitative explanatory approach was employed using survey data collected from 311 civil servants. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results show that transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards positively and significantly influence job performance. Both variables also have significant positive effects on affective commitment, which in turn enhances job performance. Furthermore, affective commitment partially mediates the relationships between transformational leadership, intrinsic rewards, and job performance. These findings highlight the importance of leadership practices and intrinsic motivational factors in strengthening employee commitment and improving performance in public sector institutions. The study provides empirical evidence from Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia and offers practical implications for performance management in bureaucratic contexts.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered technologies are increasingly being employed to help EFL students with academic writing. However, research into the combined use of DeepL and QuillBot during the writing process is sparse. This study looks on students' use and perceptions of DeepL and QuillBot in academic writing. Using a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were gathered from 49 English Education students through a 35-item five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with nine participants and analysed thematically. The data revealed that both instruments were generally viewed positively. DeepL was mostly utilized for translation and phrase improvement during planning and drafting, while QuillBot helped with paraphrasing and editing. Students did not rely solely on AI results; rather, they critically analyzed and corrected generated texts. The study finds that DeepL and QuillBot serve as supportive tools that improve academic writing while allowing students to retain control over content and meaning.

Mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and learning engagement are central to children's mathematics learning, yet their longitudinal interplay remains insufficiently understood. This study examined dynamic associations among these constructs by following 3354 Chinese third- to fifth-grade students across three waves: December 2024, June 2025, and December 2025. To capture dimension-specific processes, six random-intercept cross-lagged panel models were estimated by crossing two dimensions of mathematics anxiety (learning and evaluation) with three dimensions of learning engagement (behavioral, cognitive, and emotional). Results indicated that within-person increases in mathematics learning and evaluation anxiety were prospectively associated with decreases in subsequent academic grit and learning engagement across dimensions. Within-person increases in behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement generally predicted lower subsequent mathematics anxiety and higher academic grit. Academic grit showed reciprocal associations with mathematics anxiety and indirectly linked mathematics anxiety to subsequent behavioral engagement; however, corresponding indirect effects involving cognitive and emotional engagement were less consistent. Educational relevance and implications statement This study followed Chinese upper elementary school children over one year to understand how mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and mathematics learning engagement develop together. The findings showed that when children experienced higher levels of mathematics anxiety, whether during learning or evaluation, they tended to show lower subsequent academic grit and lower behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement in mathematics. In turn, greater engagement was followed by greater academic grit and lower mathematics anxiety. Moreover, behavioral, cognitive and emotional learning engagement were indirectly associated with lower subsequent mathematics evaluation anxiety through academic grit. These findings suggest that, in mathematics education, encouraging children to “try harder” or exert greater behavioral effort in mathematics is valuable but may not be sufficient. Teachers should also carefully design instructional materials and learning activities that foster children's emotional and cognitive engagement in mathematics. Such efforts may support the development of academic grit and potentially contribute to reducing mathematics anxiety, particularly in evaluation situations.

Despite AI-driven algorithms simplifying C2C resale platforms, adoption rates among target users (predominantly mothers) for unused baby products remain low. This study decodes this resistance by integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior and Protection Motivation Theory within a two-stage mixed-methods design (qualitative interviews, N = 37; quantitative survey, N = 670) identifies three patterns refining technology adoption frameworks. First, we reveal a “paradox of subjective complexity”: platform operational self-efficacy remains the strongest predictor of adoption intention, overriding objective technological ease and demonstrating a persistent decoupling between automated simplicity and subjective capability beliefs. Second, perceived AI functionality efficacy serves as a cognitive precondition that significantly enhances users’ internalization of social proof. Third, spatial and economic threats were indirectly associated with adoption intention through perceived platform value, suggesting a pragmatic, threat-coping pathway to circular economy participation. These insights offer actionable blueprints for policymakers and platform designers: collaborative interfaces, explainable AI (XAI), and user competence scaffolding.

With the rapid landing of XR technology in the fields of architecture, education, medical and other fields, how to effectively guide user behavior through interaction design and content mechanism has become the core topic of human-computer interaction research. This paper examines how gamification mechanisms in an XR immersive environment influence users' behavioral intentions. Drawing on self-determination theory as the overarching framework and incorporating spatial narrative structure and the Octalysis framework, it systematically examines the mediating roles of the three basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—in the immersive experience. The study uses a combination of literature review and theoretical analysis, and constructs a theoretical model of "gamification elements → psychological needs to meet → willingness to act" through the depth analysis of typical XR cases such as medical training, building space guide, safety education and other types of XR cases. The study suggests that XR's distinctive sense of presence and interactivity may amplify the psychological effects of gamification drivers, such as a sense of mission and progression, while excessive competition and manipulative design may undermine intrinsic motivation.

I am an undergraduate Psychology student at Universitas Negeri Surabaya with an interest in psychological research related to technology and education. My research focuses on the relationship between dependence on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and students' confidence in completing academic tasks. …

The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly changed the way university students access information, understand academic materials, develop ideas, and complete assignments. Tools such as ChatGPT provide students with quick explanations, summaries, and feedback that can support their learning processes. However, the increasing accessibility of these tools also raises concerns about students' potential dependency on AI and its relationship with their willingness to think critically and independently. This study aims to examine the relationship between generative AI dependency and critical thinking disposition among undergraduate students from various academic disciplines. Generative AI dependency refers to the tendency to rely excessively on AI tools when completing academic tasks or performing cognitive activities. Meanwhile, critical thinking disposition refers to an individual's willingness to evaluate information, examine evidence, consider alternative perspectives, question assumptions, and reconsider conclusions based on relevant evidence. This research uses a quantitative approach with a correlational and cross-sectional design. Data will be collected through online self-report questionnaires distributed to active undergraduate students who have used generative AI for academic purposes. The study will measure generative AI dependency as the independent variable and critical thinking disposition as the dependent variable. The collected data will be analyzed using statistical software, such as JASP, with Pearson's or Spearman's correlation analysis selected according to the characteristics of the data. The findings are expected to contribute to the fields of cognitive psychology and educational psychology by providing additional empirical evidence regarding the relationship between generative AI dependency and critical thinking disposition. The results may also help students, lecturers, and educational institutions better understand the importance of using generative AI responsibly while maintaining independent reasoning, information evaluation, and active cognitive engagement. Since the study employs a correlational design, its findings will indicate statistical relationships rather than establish a causal relationship between the two variables.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping teaching and learning in Higher Education (HE). It is central to the future of work; proficiency in the use of AI is now identified as a core employability competency and an in-demand skill for employers. Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) face a growing imperative to equip students with relevant skills, advancing their AI literacy and digital career readiness. Generative AI (GAI) tools are increasingly used in the classroom, by both staff and students, presenting a range of new challenges and opportunities for the sector. However, the integration of GAI into teaching and learning brings with it environmental costs. This chapter explores the sustainability issues posed by using GAI in the classroom and considers the implications for HEIs. It will discuss the inherent tension between meeting student needs for AI literacy, whilst also ensuring an ethical and sustainable approach to the use of GAI in teaching and learning. This chapter will argue that educators must not only teach with GAI tools as they are now an inevitable part of the future of work, but also teach about them, including their sustainability risks. The chapter concludes with recommendations for HEIs for the integration of environmental sustainability into teaching and learning surrounding GAI.

The intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainability offers a revolution in the way we address environmental emergencies and teach our children and grandchildren to tackle them. This final chapter details with the key relationship between the disciplines and suggests that AI is used to analyse complex data and model ecological systems, which is essential to solve problems such as climate change and resource depletion. The discussion is organised into three main points. The first is a discussion about the growing significance of AI as a tool for decoding the complexity of “wicked” environmental problems. Second, it highlights the top trends in the future such as AI-driven predictive modeling for climate tipping points, lifecycle assessments for circular economies and the emerging role of generative AI to redefine sustainability pedagogy and communication. Third, it emphasises some of the pressing research needs, including reducing AI’s own environmental impact, combating algorithmic bias to enable equitable solutions and designing effective pedagogies to use. In times of mounting pressure to meet climate objectives, this interconnectedness will emerge as a hallmark, and become the backbone, of a human intelligence-as-machine relationship, facilitated through precision education and cultivation, to build an equitable and regenerative future.
